title: IBM, AMD advance quantum error correction decoding at scale
content: Quantum Research Blog IBM, AMD advance quantum error correction decoding at scale New open-source tool from IBM and AMD helps researchers evaluate quantum error-correction decoders at scale for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. Date 16 Nov 2026 Authors Blake Johnson Robert Davis Topics Software Research Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: IBM and AMD released Pelagos, a new open-source framework for evaluating quantum error-correction decoders at scale. Pelagos uses GPU acceleration to help researchers run large decoder-evaluation campaigns more efficiently across modern computing infrastructure. New research demonstrates efficient multi-GPU scaling for Pelagos on AMD Instinct™ accelerators and ORNL HPC systems. An accompanying survey paper examines the growing role of decoding systems, classical infrastructure, and hardware-software co-design in fault-tolerant quantum computing. Together, these efforts support the IBM-AMD vision for quantum-centric supercomputing and the recently launched quantum error-correction co-design platform. Earlier this month, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and AMD announced a new quantum error-correction co-design platform that brings together IBM quantum processors and AMD-powered HPC infrastructure. At SC26, the collaboration is taking another step toward that vision with the open-source release of Pelagos , a GPU-accelerated framework designed to help researchers evaluate quantum error-correction decoders at scale. Dealing with quantum computers means dealing with quantum errors. To make quantum computing useful at scale, we must detect and correct those errors continuously—and much of the computational work surrounding that process happens on classical computers. As quantum error correction advances, proving that a decoder works becomes increasingly computationally demanding. Researchers often need to evaluate billions of sampled error patterns to understand how a decoder performs under realistic conditions. Those studies can require large simulation campaigns and substantial classical computing resources. Pelagos was built to make that work faster, more scalable, and more accessible to the broader research community. Alongside the Pelagos release, IBM and AMD are publishing new research demonstrating how the framework scales efficiently across multiple GPUs, including deployments on AMD-powered HPC systems. An accompanying survey paper places these developments in a broader context, highlighting the growing importance of classical infrastructure, decoding systems, and hardware-software co-design in the future of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Its central message is that fault-tolerant quantum computing will require advances not just in quantum hardware, but also in the classical systems responsible for decoding, orchestration, and data movement. The path to fault-tolerant quantum computing is an enormous classical-computing challenge, requiring CPUs, GPUs and sophisticated software to process, evaluate and ultimately help correct errors at tremendous scale. That's where IBM and AMD see an opportunity to bring together leadership quantum technology and high-performance classical computing. Accelerating decoder research with Pelagos Quantum computers are inherently susceptible to errors, making quantum error correction a foundational requirement for useful large-scale quantum computing. Error-correcting codes protect quantum information by continuously checking for signs that an error has occurred. Those checks generate data known as syndromes, which identify where an error may have happened without revealing the underlying quantum information itself. A decoder analyzes those syndromes and determines the most likely correction. As codes grow larger and researchers push toward lower logical error rates, evaluating decoder performance requires increasingly large simulation campaigns and substantial classical computing resources. Pelagos, named after the Greek word for “open sea,” is designed to help researchers navigate the challenge of decoder evaluation. Developing better decoders is essential for reliable quantum computing, but evaluating them can be extraordinarily expensive. Pelagos accelerates this workflow by combining GPU acceleration with a developer-friendly software architecture. Built using the Triton programming framework , it supports both AMD and NVIDIA GPU environments while providing a common platform for large-scale decoder evaluation. Built as an open-source framework, Pelagos gives researchers an approachable, reusable foundation for developing and evaluating new decoder algorithms. The result is a tool designed for quantum error-correction researchers, decoder developers, and HPC practitioners alike. Earlier studies showed Pelagos delivering up to 97× higher throughput than a single CPU core and performance comparable to hundreds of CPU cores for decoder-evaluation workloads.
